item.text:
Below is a drafting review of the supplied text, not a verification of the bill’s official status. Some issues are direct loopholes; others are ambiguities or missing enforcement provisions that would invite litigation or impede implementation.

### Definitions and coverage

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” permits fragmented training.** A developer could divide training among successive runs, checkpoints, subsidiaries, or cooperating models, keeping each run below the threshold. The bill does not aggregate related training, fine-tuning, or other compute used to produce a system.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—The compute threshold can miss dangerous systems.** Algorithmic improvements could produce superintelligent capabilities using less than \(10^{26}\) operations. Such systems would fall outside the compute definition and depend on an affirmative designation under § 2(1)(B).

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is excluded.** “Greater than” leaves a run at precisely the threshold outside coverage. Measurement uncertainty makes the absence of a defined counting methodology especially consequential.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is undefined.** The text does not specify how to count mixed-precision arithmetic, sparsity, failed runs, auxiliary models, synthetic-data generation, or other training-related computation. Companies could adopt accounting methods that minimize reported operations.

5. **§§ 2(1)(A), 3(a)—The point at which prohibited training begins is unclear.** The definition describes a model already “trained using” compute above the threshold, while the prohibition seeks to prevent training it. A company could argue that its model is not covered until the threshold is crossed, complicating intervention before a dangerous run is substantially complete.

6. **§ 2(1)—Key technical terms are undefined.** “Artificial intelligence model,” “artificial intelligence system,” and “training run” have no statutory boundaries. Whether ensembles, agents, scaffolding, tool use, or distributed systems constitute one covered system could determine coverage.

7. **§ 2(1)(B)—The capability standard is indeterminate.** “Substantially exceeding human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” leave the comparison population, task universe, and required margin unspecified. This creates inconsistent classification and fair-notice concerns, particularly for criminal enforcement.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—Dangerous specialized systems may escape.** A system capable of catastrophic cyber operations, biological design, or autonomous AI research might not exceed humans across “most cognitive tasks.” The definition does not independently capture such narrower but dangerous capabilities.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—Coverage depends on a government determination.** Unlike the compute limb, the capability limb requires the Secretary to act; a company could argue that an otherwise qualifying system remains lawful until designated. There is no deadline or provisional restriction while a determination is pending.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is not identified.** Commerce is mentioned elsewhere, but the Act never expressly assigns this designation authority to the Secretary of Commerce. That omission creates avoidable uncertainty over who may make legally operative determinations.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—No designation procedure or testing authority is supplied.** The bill specifies neither required evidence and testing access nor notice, reconsideration, and review procedures. Companies could conceal capabilities or contest designations, while the government lacks an express mechanism to compel the information needed to classify systems.

12. **§ 2(2)—“U.S. person” excludes major categories of domestic actors abroad.** The definition omits lawful permanent residents and entities such as LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and unincorporated associations; it also does not expressly include corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Those omissions weaken the prohibition’s overseas reach.

13. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign affiliates provide a route around overseas coverage.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary of a U.S. company is not itself a “U.S. person” under this definition. The bill does not expressly prohibit a domestic parent from directing, financing, or arranging prohibited foreign activity through such entities.

14. **§ 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** There is no technical specification, performance standard, or updating mechanism. Operators could dispute whether particular accelerators, custom hardware, or future architectures count.

15. **§ 2(3)—The facility threshold is easily avoided.** A facility containing exactly 50,000 qualifying chips is excluded, and substantial prohibited training may be possible with fewer chips. The registry therefore does not reliably capture facilities capable of conducting covered activity.

16. **§ 2(3)—Distributed infrastructure is not aggregated.** Operators could split chips across data centers or separately characterized facilities, each below the threshold. “Data center” and facility boundaries are undefined, inviting disputes over campuses, buildings, and shared installations.

### Prohibition and exceptions

17. **§ 3(a)—Important enabling conduct is not expressly prohibited.** Financing, procuring compute, supplying model weights, providing technical assistance, or arranging another actor’s work may fall outside “train, develop, or deploy.” Existing accessory doctrines may address some conduct, but the bill supplies no comprehensive civil prohibition on facilitation or circumvention.

18. **§ 3(a)—Possession, transfer, and continued operation are unclear.** The text does not expressly prohibit acquiring, retaining, distributing, or running a covered system after deployment. “Deploy” might encompass some continuing uses, but leaving that question implicit creates an unnecessary enforcement dispute.

19. **§ 3(a)—Domestic territorial coverage is underspecified for remote activity.** The bill does not say how it applies when a foreign actor remotely controls U.S. compute, or when development spans several countries. Explicit rules for conduct using domestic infrastructure would reduce disputes about where the prohibited activity occurs.

20. **§ 3(a)—There is no express rule for federal agencies or government contractors.** Whether “any person” reaches the United States itself is uncertain, and contractor activity could raise additional disputes. If government development is intended to be prohibited, the statute should say so expressly.

21. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering exempts entire systems, not merely completed historical conduct.** Any covered system whose training began before enactment appears exempt from the whole prohibition. That permits continued training, development, and deployment after enactment, potentially indefinitely.

22. **§ 3(b)—Starting a token training run could secure an exemption.** Nothing requires substantial progress, a specified project scope, or documented commencement. Developers could initiate many nominal runs before enactment and later claim that much larger projects were grandfathered.

23. **§ 3(b)—Model lineage and modification are unaddressed.** The bill does not define when fine-tuning, retraining, merging, distillation, or architectural changes produce a new system rather than an exempt old one. Companies could characterize successive, increasingly capable versions as the same grandfathered system.

24. **§ 3(b)—No proof or registration requirement supports grandfathering.** The text does not require contemporaneous training records, notification, or identification of exempt systems. This makes commencement dates and claimed exemptions difficult to verify.

25. **§ 3(c)—The safety-evaluation exception is exceptionally broad.** It exempts “activities” conducted for that purpose without limiting the actor, scale, duration, or resulting capabilities. A developer could characterize otherwise prohibited training or deployment as necessary to evaluate safety.

26. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activity is not addressed.** The text does not require safety evaluation to be the sole or primary purpose. Commercial development accompanied by a safety-testing objective could therefore claim the exemption.

27. **§ 3(c)—There are no authorization or containment requirements.** The exception requires no independent evaluator, advance approval, secure environment, reporting, or restriction on releasing weights and results. Even genuinely safety-motivated work could create or disseminate the systems the bill seeks to prohibit.

### Registry and enforcement

28. **§ 4(a)—Registration has no deadline or required contents.** The bill does not state when existing or newly qualifying facilities must register, what information they must provide, or how changes must be reported. Those omissions make compliance and enforcement uncertain.

29. **§ 4—The responsible “operator” is undefined.** Facility owners, cloud providers, tenants, and compute customers may each control different aspects of the infrastructure. Without allocating duties, each could argue that another entity must register or provide workload information.

30. **§ 4(b)—Reporting applies only to “registered” operators.** An operator that fails to register could argue that the reporting obligation never attaches. The duty should apply to every operator required to register, regardless of actual registration.

31. **§ 4(b)—Quarterly workload descriptions are too unspecified to ensure detection.** The bill requires no standardized compute accounting, customer identification, model lineage, training dates, or supporting records. Generic descriptions could satisfy the literal requirement without revealing prohibited activity, and quarterly reporting may arrive too late to prevent a completed run.

32. **§ 4—No verification or record-preservation mechanism is supplied.** There are no express inspection, audit, subpoena, telemetry, or record-retention requirements. Operator certification alone gives the government little ability to verify omissions or misleading reports.

33. **§§ 4–5—Registry violations have no express penalties.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of § 3, not failures to register, report, or preserve evidence. Other generally applicable laws might reach some false statements, but they do not replace a complete registry-enforcement scheme.

34. **§§ 3–5—Enforcement responsibility and civil procedures are missing.** The bill does not clearly assign investigative and penalty-assessment authority or establish procedures for hearings, collection, and agency referral. It also lacks an express rulemaking grant for implementing the technical and reporting requirements.

35. **§§ 3–5—There is no express emergency shutdown or injunction mechanism.** Monetary penalties and prosecution may arrive after a prohibited system has been created. The bill should clearly authorize appropriate preventive judicial relief, including orders stopping training or deployment, rather than leave officials to argue for implied remedies.

36. **§ 5(a)—The civil penalty may be an affordable business expense.** The maximum is $1 million per day, with no minimum, revenue-based alternative, or express recovery of gains. For a major AI company, expected returns could exceed even the maximum exposure.

37. **§ 5(a)—The unit and duration of a violation are unclear.** The text does not specify whether simultaneous systems create separate penalties or whether retaining or operating a completed system constitutes an ongoing violation. Companies could argue for one daily cap covering all activity or penalties limited to a brief training or deployment event.

38. **§ 5(b)—“Willfully” creates a potentially demanding proof requirement.** Its precise meaning would depend on judicial interpretation, but defendants may argue that prosecutors must prove awareness that their conduct was unlawful. Ambiguous definitions and exceptions would make that proof harder.

39. **§§ 2, 3, 5(b)—Criminal liability rests partly on uncertain or discretionary coverage.** Undefined technical terms and capability designations create potential due-process challenges concerning notice and vagueness. The bill should clarify when designations become binding and how regulated parties can ascertain coverage before criminal liability attaches.

40. **§§ 3–5—Overseas prohibitions lack supporting enforcement arrangements.** Expressly covering U.S. persons abroad does not itself secure foreign evidence, access to facilities, or cooperation from foreign authorities. The bill supplies no specific overseas reporting or cooperation mechanisms to support that reach.

### International agreement, duration, and effective date

41. **§ 6—The international-agreement obligation is only an obligation to seek negotiations.** It does not require an agreement to be concluded, implemented, or enforced, and the placement of “not later than 18 months” leaves the required milestone unclear. There are no interim measures addressing foreign development while negotiations proceed.

42. **§ 6—“Equivalent” prohibitions could reproduce the domestic loopholes.** The required agreement is tied to § 3, including its grandfathering and safety-evaluation exceptions, without requiring equivalent definitions, monitoring, or enforcement. Countries could adopt nominally similar prohibitions with materially weaker coverage.

43. **§ 7(a)—The early-termination safety standard is undefined.** “Can be developed safely” does not specify acceptable risk, evidence, verification, or whether safety applies to all covered systems or only a particular method. A narrow finding about one approach could be invoked to justify ending the entire prohibition.

44. **§ 7(a)—The National Academies report requirement is procedurally incomplete.** The bill does not commission a report or specify its scope, independence safeguards, publication, or necessary findings. “Acting on a report” could permit reliance on a report that does not actually establish the safety of ending the prohibition.

45. **§ 7(a)—Termination is not linked to international compliance and has no automatic reversal.** Congress could lift the prohibition without an effective international enforcement regime. Once lifted, the text provides no mechanism to restore it if the safety finding proves wrong or circumstances change.

46. **§ 7(b)—The ten-year sunset overrides the safety condition.** The entire Act expires after ten years whether or not Congress finds development safe under § 7(a). Companies could simply wait out the prohibition.

47. **§ 7(b)—Sunsetting the entire Act creates enforcement-transition problems.** Registration and reporting cease along with the prohibition, and there is no tailored provision governing pending matters or retained records. The general federal saving statute may preserve accrued liabilities, but it does not substitute for an orderly transition scheme.

48. **§§ 5(a), 8—The penalty date conflicts with the effective date.** Civil penalties are specified for violations occurring on or after enactment, but the Act takes effect only 180 days later. That creates uncertainty over whether pre-effective-date activity can be penalized and invites retroactivity and fair-notice objections.

49. **§§ 3(b), 8—The delayed effective date creates a development window.** Companies can continue otherwise covered activity during the 180-day period before the prohibition takes effect. Although systems first trained during that interval are not expressly grandfathered, the delay allows development and dissemination before enforceable restrictions begin.
